thread.title: Scientists Discover New Ice Age Toad Species in La Brea Tar Pits, Second Extinct Amphibian Ever Found in North America
thread.title_full: Scientists Discover New Ice Age Toad Species in La Brea Tar Pits, Second Extinct Amphibian Ever Found in North America

author: Renz Soliman
title: Scientists Discover New Ice Age Toad Species in La Brea Tar Pits, Second Extinct Amphibian Ever Found in North America
text:
Scientists have identified a new extinct Ice Age spadefoot toad, Spea labreae, from fossils at Los Angeles' La Brea Tar Pits, marking only the second known extinct Pleistocene amphibian ever found in North America.
The newly described species was recognized from small hip and spine fragments, known as the sacro-urostyle, that had been stored in museum collections since they were excavated from Rancho La Brea in 1929.
Paleontologist José Alberto Cruz, the study's lead author, reexamined the bones while reviewing amphibian material from the tar pits and noticed features that did not match any known spadefoot toad species, according to CNN.
A New Ice Age Toad Fossil
By comparing the fossil element with modern spadefoot toads from different regions, Cruz and coauthor Emily Lindsey concluded that the remains represented a previously unknown species and formally named it Spea labreae in a paper published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.
Scientists say Spea labreae is scientifically significant because extinct amphibians are extremely rare in the North American fossil record, which has been dominated by large mammals such as mammoths, saber-toothed cats and dire wolves.
According to the researchers, this toad is only the second extinct Pleistocene amphibian documented from the continent, alongside a tree frog species identified from Florida, making the La Brea Tar Pits discovery a notable expansion of known Ice Age biodiversity.

It is also the first extinct amphibian ever confirmed from Ice Age Los Angeles, showing that the site preserves more delicate vertebrate fossils than previously appreciated.
The fossil's exact age cannot be determined without destructive testing, but its context within La Brea deposits indicates it lived during the last Ice Age interval for which the tar pits have been active, roughly within the past 60,000 years, Scientific American reported.
Analyzing the New Finding
Amphibians such as spadefoot toads are considered useful indicators of ancient environments because they are sensitive to moisture and temperature and typically remain close to their breeding and burrowing sites.
Researchers say the presence of Spea labreae in prehistoric Los Angeles suggests cooler, wetter conditions than those found in the region today and contributes data that may refine reconstructions of local Ice Age climate.
In the same study, Cruz and Lindsey also reported the first fossil evidence that the Mexican burrowing toad, Rhinophrynus dorsalis, once lived in the southwestern United States, even though the species is now restricted to southern Mexico.
Together, the new spadefoot toad and the burrowing toad fossils broaden the picture of Ice Age amphibian diversity at La Brea Tar Pits and underscore the scientific value of reexamining long-stored specimens in museum collections.
The authors note that ongoing work at the Samuel Oschin Global Center for Ice Age Research at La Brea Tar Pits continues to uncover previously overlooked species, adding detail to how life and climate changed in and around Los Angeles at the end of the last Ice Age, as per Phys.
